deep-tech-efd652a2c2.fulltext:

Government agencies and companies around the world shut down websites on Wednesday after two critical flaws came to light involving PHP, a programming language that is the basis for a large share of the internet.
PHP sits underneath popular web design platforms, so the weaknesses potentially affect a vast range of websites, from online stores and news outlets to government services.
Wiz, one of the security firms that found the issues, estimated that PHP runs about 70 per cent of the world’s websites and said the flaws rank “among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP and arguably in software history”.
The US National Security Agency told organisations to patch immediately or pull vulnerable systems offline. The flaws “often provide a direct path to the server’s file system or database”, the NSA said in a statement on social media.
Attackers could use them to take over web servers without needing a password.
Volker Dusch, a security engineer at the PHP Foundation, told The Wall Street Journal it was the most serious problem PHP had faced in more than a decade, comparing it to Heartbleed, a 2014 flaw that set off a worldwide rush to patch.
The discovery came amid a surge in software security disclosures driven by increasingly powerful AI models, with the number of vulnerabilities found in 2026 on track to roughly double last year’s record total.
“If you run PHP, it is imperative that you update now,” the PHP Foundation, which funds developers working on the language, said in a blog post.
Security firm Calif found the flaws in August using OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol model, as part of an OpenAI-funded audit of PHP’s code.
Google-owned Wiz said it found them independently weeks later with help from AI models including Google’s Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol.
OpenAI said on social media that it considered the bug “one of the most impactful vulnerabilities in recent memory”, adding that it “marks a new phase, where AI can find security bugs with internet-scale impact.”
Ethan Mollick, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School who studies AI, said that companies he talks to are struggling to keep up with the pace of patches needed to shield from AI-driven cyberattacks.
“Now consumers are going to have the same experience of getting everything updated often and fast,” he said on social media.
The flaws had been reported privately to PHP’s developers and kept confidential while a fix was prepared.
Details leaked online on Tuesday, a day before the planned release of the fix, prompting the rush to take sites offline.
In France, local government websites, including one for Paris police, have been inaccessible since Wednesday afternoon at the request of the French National Cybersecurity Agency, the interior ministry said.
In the Netherlands, the national digital identity service DigiD, the website of the House of Representatives and the site of the national cybersecurity centre went offline as a precaution, according to Dutch public broadcaster NOS.
Belgium’s foreign ministry temporarily took its websites offline as a precaution, it said on social media, although the Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium had recorded no attacks on Belgian sites.
In Australia, the Australian Signals Directorate said its own cyber.gov.au site was among government websites affected by the flaws, according to public broadcaster ABC.

world-9e5f09d152.headline: China’s Free A.I. Models Are Thrown Into Uncertainty
world-9e5f09d152.fulltext:
Draft rules on the export of artificial intelligence technology show how China is trying to balance national security risks with its desire to outpace the United States.
Under rules proposed last week, the next advanced A.I. models might need the government’s permission to be exported out of China.
When the Chinese start-up Moonshot AI in July released Kimi K3, an artificial intelligence model that rivaled some of the best systems made by American companies, it was free for anyone to download.
By making advanced A.I. models easily available, Chinese companies have turned open access into one of China’s most powerful advantages in its rivalry with the United States to shape the future of the technology.
Now Beijing is moving to tighten its grip on the global spread of the country’s top-tier A.I., proposing rules that could give the government new power to track, and potentially limit, where the systems go.
At the same time, the government sought to reassure users that the move would not stifle access to Chinese A.I., saying the vast majority of the technology would still be freely exported.
The draft rules reflect Beijing’s effort to balance two competing goals: regulate the spread of its frontier A.I. systems for strategic and security reasons while still encouraging global users to adopt Chinese software.
“It is almost like you have two voices speaking at the same time,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution focusing on Chinese technology and industrial policy. “One saying, ‘We want extra control of these sensitive technologies so that they can’t hurt China’ and another voice saying, ‘We want to develop the best A.I. technology and we want to share it with the rest of the world.’”
David Pierson covers Chinese foreign policy and China’s economic and cultural engagement with the world. He has been a journalist for more than two decades.
Adam Satariano is a technology correspondent for The Times, based in London.

global-economics-ba060f091f.headline: Tesla and SpaceX explore merger as Elon Musk gives backing
global-economics-ba060f091f.fulltext:
As SpaceX released its second-ever public earnings report on Tuesday, Elon Musk declared his support for combining the aerospace and AI company with his electric vehicle company, Tesla. He said both companies had created special committees to explore a potential merger, but have not reached any agreement on terms of a transaction.
“Both SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss this idea at the request of shareholders and these special committees are, uh, consist of independent directors,” Musk said on the call. “Because I’m a conflicted party, I can’t actually be in the discussions of the special committees.”
Musk also expressed his backing for the move, while cautioning about the hurdles involved achieve it. He stated that it would require the approval of 50% of all Tesla shareholders.
“I think some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty and I think that would be overstating it,” Musk said, adding it would require shareholder approvals and special committees at both firms. “I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies.”
The company revealed a far better financial quarter than Wall Street projected. SpaceX company, which encompasses rockets, artificial intelligence and satellite communications, reported a 161% growth in revenue year over year, driven by its Starlink and AI segments.
The company declared $14.58bn in revenue against analysts’ projected $12.72bn. SpaceX reported earnings per share of 35 cents and a net income of $4.4bn. The company’s stock, which started the day down about 8% for the year, shot up 2% in after hours trading immediately after the results.
Musk appeared alongside SpaceX’s president, Gwynne Shotwell, and CFO, Bret Johnsen, at his Starlink factory in Texas to deliver the earnings report, touting the company’s growth and plans for future rocket developments. Musk also highlighted its artificial intelligence segment, which the company refers to as Super Intelligence, that drew $7.6bn in revenue and now outperforms its Connectivity business, which provides internet services.
Musk’s company once again found itself in the spotlight in recent weeks as investors have speculated about the potential merger with Tesla, the second-most valuable part of the tech mogul’s empire. Musk has also been at the center of geopolitical tensions after Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukraine’s president, last week accused SpaceX of restricting access to its military-grade Starlink internet service.
The disruption in service to Starshield allegedly led to several failed Ukrainian combat missions and left the country more vulnerable to Russian drone attacks, as well as highlighted how global internet infrastructure has come to rely on Musk’s products. Musk denied responsibility for the disruption, stating that Starshield was controlled by the US government, not SpaceX. The White House has likewise denied hobbling Starshield.
Moments before the SpaceX earnings call on Tuesday, the Wall Street Journal reported that Musk personally ordered the throttling of Starshield, citing unnamed US officials and people familiar with the matter. Musk faced no questions about the reports on the investor Q&A portion of SpaceX’s earnings call.
While SpaceX’s role in international affairs faces scrutiny, Musk has taken on a resurgent role in US domestic politics. The world’s richest person has contributed $366m in political spending this election cycle, backing Republican-aligned Super Pacs and pouring money into influencing key midterm races. Musk also agreed earlier this month to co-lead a Pentagon project on the future of warfare, bringing him back into government work after his time as the de facto leader of the so-called “department of government efficiency” (Doge).
Musk recently pledged to give every child in the US one of his SpaceX stocks next year, which Donald Trump stated would be facilitated through the president’s “Trump accounts” initiative that creates savings plans for children. The prospective share giveaway is a rare display of philanthropy from Musk, who has criticized traditional aid organizations and has taken credit for dismantling the world’s largest single provider of humanitarian aid by gutting the government agency USAID.
“Giving shares, which are stakes in the future economy, directly to the people is the way,” Musk posted on X, the social media company he owns.
Tech leaders such as Musk have faced increasing public pushback over their extraordinary accumulation of wealth and power in the US, while this year AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic both announced big investments to their grant-making and non-profit arms. Musk’s announcement came after Anthropic announced earlier this week that it plans to donate 5% of its shares to a newly created public benefit fund within the company.
Tesla will also reveal its latest earnings this week, with Musk set to deliver the quarterly report on Wednesday. The company’s stock received a slight boost this week after it unveiled its new Tesla Roadster 2 electric sports car, which Musk showcased in a dramatic demonstration that included the vehicle using pressurized air tanks to briefly lift off the ground and perform aerial stunts.

india-a582d2ca1a.headline: Marco Rubio in India: Trade deal in sight, oil on the agenda
india-a582d2ca1a.fulltext:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said India and the United States were “very, very close” to finalising a trade deal, with only a few issues left to resolve, during his two-day visit to India on October 20-21. His meetings also focused on expanding energy trade, including the possibility of Indian refineries processing more Venezuelan crude.
“I would say we're about as close as you can be without having executed the agreement,” Rubio told reporters in Mumbai on Tuesday. “I think there's a small number of items to wrap up, so I think that will happen shortly.” He said the US was optimistic about reaching an agreement soon, but did not give a date for its conclusion.
US President Donald Trump also said on Tuesday that the two countries were “pretty close” to an agreement. “They want to make a deal. We're going to make a deal. Pretty close, yeah,” he told reporters at the White House, adding that it would be “a much different kind of deal” from previous agreements, without elaborating.
Rubio also met External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar in Mumbai before travelling to Jamnagar in Gujarat the following day to visit Reliance Industries' refining complex. After the meeting, Jaishankar said the two sides discussed trade, energy, technology, defence, people-to-people ties, and regional developments.
“Pleased to meet US Secretary Rubio in Mumbai today. We shared views on further advancing our ties, focusing on trade, energy, technology, defence, and people-to-people ties. Also exchanged views on regional developments,” Jaishankar said in a post on X. India's Ministry of External Affairs said both sides had welcomed progress in negotiations on the India-US Bilateral Trade Agreement and reaffirmed their commitment to working towards its early conclusion.
Trade Talks
Trade negotiations between India and the US have been ongoing since Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, with differences over tariffs and market access delaying an agreement. India's continued purchases of Russian crude have added to tensions between the two countries.
Washington is seeking greater access to India's market and ways to address its trade deficit, while New Delhi has pushed for preferential access for Indian exporters and greater certainty over US tariffs.
Earlier this month, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said the negotiations had reached a “plateau”, with further concessions likely to be “very, very difficult” for both sides. She said the talks were continuing and noted that addressing the US trade deficit with India was a major consideration for Washington.
On October 15, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said the first phase of the bilateral trade agreement had been finalised and was undergoing legal drafting. He said India wanted to secure a competitive advantage over peer countries before the agreement was operationalised.
US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor had also said last week that the broad framework and major elements of the agreement were settled, though work on the remaining issues continued.
Rubio said that both sides needed to agree on the meaning of the language before announcing a deal. In an interview with Network18, on Tuesday, he explained, “The difference is when you are friends, when you are allies, when you have so much in common, that's what allows you to bridge those differences and come up with something that's mutually beneficial.” Rubio added that the negotiations had reached the stage of working through technical details. He said, “I'm not personally negotiating it because it's done through our Trade Representative. But I know, and have been very involved in watching it happen, that it is something we anticipate seeing in a matter of weeks, not months.”
Reliance, Venezuelan crude and energy talks
Speaking to reporters in Mumbai, Rubio said India had repeatedly expressed a desire to diversify its energy sources. “It's not easy to do that from one day to the next,” he said, adding that India had made “some substantial progress” and that the US could supply some of its energy needs.
“We have discussed Venezuela and other countries, and I think it's in our interest to have strong allies with diverse energy portfolios,” he said. Rubio also said he would discuss Venezuelan crude with Reliance. The company has processed the country's heavy crude in the past and has refining capacity suited to those grades.
“They've done so in the past. They have the capability to refine heavy crude,” Rubio said. “As more and more Venezuelan oil comes online, it's something they can do.”
He also referred to oil concessions held by Indian companies in Venezuela and said they could increase production there. Rubio said sanctions could present obstacles that would need to be addressed.
During his visit to Jamnagar on Wednesday, Rubio said the visit was an opportunity to see Reliance's operations and discuss its presence in global energy markets. Reliance operates two refineries at Jamnagar, with a combined crude-processing capacity of about 1.4 million barrels per day.
Rubio's visit comes as the US-Iran war has continued to push energy costs higher. Renewed attacks on shipping and energy infrastructure in West Asia have led Brent crude futures to rise above the $100 mark. On Wednesday morning, Brent rose to $110.11 a barrel, nearing a five-month high. The International Energy Agency has said global diesel and gas oil exports fell by nearly 700,000 barrels per day year on year in September, with losses from Russia and West Asia only partly offset by higher supplies elsewhere. The agency expects the diesel market to remain tight well into 2027, as supply disruptions, high shipping costs and refinery constraints limit the recovery in availability.
Russian oil and tariffs
India's purchases of Russian crude have strained relations with the United States. In September, the US passed legislation allowing tariffs of up to 100 percent on goods from major buyers of Russian oil, including India. Trump waived the relevant provisions on October 16 and announced a 60-day review period.
Rubio has said the impact of tariffs on US relations with India must be weighed alongside Washington's objectives in dealing with Russia. He has argued that energy supply, prices and countries' ability to find alternative sources need to be considered when Washington makes sanctions decisions.
New Delhi has argued that energy imports should reflect supply availability, prices, and the need to maintain market stability. The US, meanwhile, has suggested India diversify its sources, including through increased purchases of American energy.
India imports more than 85 percent of its crude oil requirements and has continued to buy Russian oil despite pressure from Washington.
During his visit, Rubio also met Adani Group chairman Gautam Adani and Tata Sons chairman N Chandrasekaran in Mumbai, paid tribute to the victims of the 26/11 Mumbai terror attacks at the Taj Mahal Palace hotel, and attended a reception marking the 250th anniversary of US independence. Rubio is scheduled to leave Jamnagar early on Thursday, October 22, concluding his visit to India.

ai-a28446b274.headline: PE funding for Indian AI start-ups has tripled in 2025: Goldman Sachs
ai-a28446b274.fulltext:
Private equity (PE) investment in Indian artificial intelligence (AI) start-ups has tripled in a year, and AI now accounts for about a fifth of all private capital deployed in the country, according to a new Goldman Sachs report.
Funding rose to roughly $5 billion in 2025 from $1.6 billion in 2024, the report noted. The pace has quickened since. The first eight to nine months of 2026 have already matched last year’s record total, putting the full year on course to surpass it. AI’s share of all PE funding has climbed from about 5 percent in 2024 to around 20 percent so far in 2026.
The bank also notes that “this scale of funding challenges a broad perception we hear from investors that India is peripheral to the global AI buildout”. Stanford University’s 2026 AI Index ranks India sixth worldwide for private AI funding in 2025, and fourth for newly funded AI companies, behind only the US, UK and China.
Goldman Sachs also screened about 7,000 unlisted companies that have raised private funding over the past 15 years and identified 84 “Private AI Contenders” in India. It estimates their combined value at about $55 billion. They account for roughly 40 percent of AI-related private capital raised in India since 2025.
Upstream enablers, covering power, semiconductors and data centres, are the largest group, at about $35 billion. Downstream adopters, which apply AI in areas such as healthcare, financial services and robotics, are worth $18 billion and make up 42 of the 84 firms. Midstream “core engine” companies, which develop foundational models, are the smallest group, at about $2 billion across seven firms. Bangalore is home to 32 of the contenders, followed by Delhi/NCR with 16, Mumbai with 12 and Hyderabad with eight.
The report also looks at which companies might list next. Of the 84 companies, 71 are at the growth, late, infrastructure or buyout stages, with a combined value of about $54 billion. Such firms have historically taken two to five years to reach the stock market, listing at valuations two to ten times their private-round levels.
Assuming that 25-50 percent of them list at an average 4x step-up, Goldman estimates that $50 billion to $100 billion in incremental market value could be added to India’s listed AI complex.
That is modest compared with the $670 billion listed AI “Enablers” cohort. The report also noted that the bigger change is in what investors could buy. Upstream companies could account for about 66 percent of potential listings, with downstream adopters accounting for about 31 percent. New segments would include data centre operators, enterprise AI services, conversational AI, cloud and data management, healthcare AI and computer vision.
Goldman cautioned that the IPO exercise is purely illustrative and that it takes no view on individual listings or valuations. It also acknowledged that its top-down screen may include false positives and miss companies without large PE or venture backing.

global-economics-043f834fd7.headline: Indian central bank rejects all bids at treasury bill auction as short-term yields surge

RBI rejects all bids at govt's T-bill auction as short-term yields surge
The yield on the benchmark 10-year government bond settled at 7.44 per cent, its highest level since November 4, 2022, against the previous close of 7.39 per cent
Listen to This Article
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Wednesday rejected all bids at the government’s treasury-bill (T-bill) auction, signalling discomfort with the sharp rise in short-term borrowing costs, dealers said. 
The yield on the benchmark 10-year government bond settled at 7.44 per cent, its highest level since November 4, 2022, against the previous close of 7.39 per cent. 
The central bank last rejected bids in June, when it cancelled auctions of 182-day and 364-day T-bills. At the end of March, it had rejected bids across all three maturities. 
The government had planned to raise ₹23,000 crore through the sale of 91-day, 182-day and 364-day T-bills. Traders said the yields sought by investors may have been higher than the RBI’s expectations. Government bonds, already under selling pressure due to rising crude oil prices and US treasury yields, were impacted further after the auction result. 
“The yield (on the benchmark 10-year government bond) will now inch up to 7.50 per cent from here. Crude remains the main overhang, with Brent trading around $112 per barrel, and US yields have also inched up. That is a worry for the market. Sentiment turned negative again after the auction result was announced,” said a dealer at a primary dealership. 
Also Read
Cutoff yields on T-bills have risen sharply over the past five weeks. Between September 9 and October 14, yields on 91-day, 182-day and 364-day bills rose by 64 basis points (bps), 83 bps and 69 bps, respectively. 
At last week’s auction, the government raised funds at yields of 5.73 per cent for 91-day bills, 6.29 per cent for 182-day bills and 6.49 per cent for 364-day bills. 
The spread between the yield on 364-day T-bills and the RBI’s policy repo rate widened to 99 bps last week, its highest level in four years, reflecting rising short-term borrowing costs.  
The central bank has turned decisively hawkish. It raised the repo rate to 5.50 per cent this month and shifted its stance to calibrated tightening, signalling the possibility of further increases. 
Bets on a 50 bps hike in December are growing, while the benchmark 10-year bond yield has risen around 20 bps since the policy announcement. 
Liquidity, which had cushioned the market for much of the year, has dried up. The RBI’s latest data showed that net liquidity in the banking system stood at a surplus of around ₹48,303 crore on Tuesday. 
Consequently, the RBI’s overnight variable rate repo (VRR) auction witnessed strong demand, with bids amounting to ₹93,241 crore against the notified amount of ₹50,000 crore. 
The weighted average call rate (WACR), the operating target of monetary policy, settled at 5.64 per cent on Wednesday, close to the marginal standing facility (MSF) rate, against 5.66 per cent in the previous session. On Monday, the RBI had conducted a ₹1 trillion VRR auction, the first in three months. 
“Liquidity has almost dried up, keeping overnight rates elevated. We also have tax outflows coming. The RBI would like to keep overnight rates aligned with the repo rate. That is why it is conducting these temporary liquidity infusions,” said a dealer at a state-owned bank. 
The turnaround in liquidity has been sharp. The RBI had been in absorption mode since August 6, following its last VRR auction on July 29, as liquidity had swelled due to Foreign Currency Non-Resident Bank, or FCNR(B), deposit swaps with the central bank. 
Since then, the daily cash reserve requirement has been tightened from October 16. Average daily net absorption under the liquidity adjustment facility rose from ₹1.2 trillion in July to ₹5.8 trillion in August. As recently as October 12, the RBI absorbed a net ₹3.36 trillion, while the call rate stood at 5.41 per cent. 
The central bank plans to conduct another overnight VRR auction worth ₹50,000 crore on Thursday.

H-1B woes: Over 12,000 Indian tech workers return from US amid visa uncertainty and layoffs - Key details here
About 12,700 Indian technology professionals had returned from the US by September 2026, putting departures on track to potentially exceed last year’s peak.
Amid Trump's visa crackdown, an increasing proportion of technology sector employees originating from India are relocating from the US to their country of origin, reported The Economic Times.
Approximately 12,700 specialists had completed this transition by September 2026, positioning the year to potentially exceed the last year's documented peak of 15,100 departures, according to information compiled by Xpheno.
The figures have demonstrated consistent growth throughout the preceding years, rising from 7,200 in 2023 to 9,800 in 2024. If this pattern continues, India may experience a scenario wherein more technology professionals are returning from the US rather than emigrating to it.
This shift is happening as people worry more about what immigration and visa rules might look like under the Trump administration. At the same time, companies are cutting jobs left and right, and the global job market feels pretty shaky, which is pushing people to make this move.
Indians returning from US to face many challenges
LinkedIn user Abhinarayan Mishra shared that heading back to India isn't necessarily a smooth transition. Mishra points out that Indian companies are really focused on hiring people with skills in artificial intelligence, cloud computing, cybersecurity, and product leadership—rather than just valuing general work experience abroad. He also mentioned some real challenges people face when returning, like dealing with tax rules in both countries, plus the tricky part of helping their Gen Z kids adjust to a new education system and lifestyle.
Also Read: Trump revokes over 300,000 visas: Here's what Indian nationals travelling to the US must know
PERM process halted for several tech firms
This development follows the halting of PERM processing for several of the world's most prominent talent acquisition companies, such as Microsoft, Adobe, Infosys, Cognizant, Capgemini, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Tata.
PERM, which stands for Program Electronic Review Management, represents a crucial component in the employer-sponsored green card pathway. Typically, it requires employers to show that qualified, readily available U.S. workers cannot be found for the role and that bringing on an international worker won't negatively impact the compensation and workplace conditions of comparable American employees.
For Indian professionals dependent on employer sponsorship, the suspension may postpone their aspirations to secure permanent residency status. The extent of this impact, nevertheless, will be contingent upon their present immigration classification and the progression of their green card petitions.
Immigration expert weighs in
According to immigration specialist Swatilina Barik, this measure does not revoke currently valid H-1B visas or invalidate green cards that have received prior approval, as per American Bazaar. It rather restricts the affected organizations from submitting new PERM applications and halts applications currently under review during the period of suspension.
Barik further emphasized that this development should be interpreted as a constraint on the employment-based permanent residency mechanism rather than a termination of temporary work visa authorization.

Legal AI startup Legora announced Wednesday that it raised a $550 million Series E round, valuing it at $8.8 billion.
The company helps automate and assist with workflow tasks for legal professionals, as the industry moves beyond AI assistants to AI services that help them get work done.
The news comes just a month after Harvey, Legora’s biggest competitor, announced a $550 million raise at a $15.5 billion valuation; back in March, Harvey also said its annual recurring revenue (ARR) was more than $ 200 million.
Legora’s Series E follows the company’s April announcement of a $50 million extension of a $550 million Series D round, which valued the company at $5.6 billion. At the time, the company said its ARR had reached $100 million. That number now stands at over $200 million, the company shared on Wednesday.
Investors in the latest financing include Atreides Management, which led the round, as well as Baron Capital, Bessemer Venture Partners, General Catalyst, Menlo, and other top names. The company plans to use the fresh capital to further expand across North America.

ai-dc1c99f797.headline: Recursive launches Flint, a laptop coding model it says was largely built by AI
ai-dc1c99f797.fulltext:
Recursive, an AI startup founded last year, is starting to live up to its name. The company, which is trying to build AI that can improve itself, released its first model, Flint, on Wednesday. Flint is a free coding model that can run on a laptop and was built largely with the help of AI.
Recursive’s automated research system, which it calls the Eureka Machine, helped with nearly every step of Flint’s development, the company says. That let a small team build the model from scratch in under four months.
Flint is an early public test of recursive self-improvement: the idea that AI can build better AI, which in turn builds even better AI. It’s also one of the most debated ideas in the industry. Some researchers fear that AI improving itself could slip out of human control. For now, Recursive’s version is more limited: an AI research assistant overseen by people that produced a model small enough for a laptop.
The company emerged from stealth in May with $650 million in funding at a $4.65 billion valuation, from backers including GV, Nvidia, and AMD Ventures. Recursive is led by CEO Richard Socher, Salesforce’s former chief scientist.
Because Flint runs on a user’s own computer rather than a company’s cloud servers, developers can use it offline, keep their code private, and avoid the usage fees that AI cloud services charge based on how much text the model processes. The model is free to download on Hugging Face, the popular site for sharing AI models, under the Apache 2.0 license, an open-source license that allows free use and modification.
Flint is a mixture-of-experts model, meaning it uses only a small slice of itself for any given task: just 2.5 billion of its 40 billion settings, known as parameters, at a time. That makes it light enough for an ordinary laptop and far smaller than Meta’s Muse Spark Open, an open model built for Macs that was released last week. Muse Spark Open uses 816 billion parameters and needs at least a terabyte of memory.
Flint is also fast. In Recursive’s tests, it generated about 131 tokens (chunks of text) per second on a MacBook Pro with Apple’s M4 Pro chip — roughly twice the 58 to 69 tokens per second that similar models managed on the same machine, including Google’s Gemma 4 and Nvidia’s Nemotron 3.5 Lightning. On Nvidia’s RTX Spark, Flint topped 150 tokens per second.
On SWE-Bench Verified, a benchmark that measures how well AI can fix real-world software bugs, Flint outperformed other models under 50 billion parameters. On Recursive’s own average across six tests, only one model, Alibaba’s Qwen3.8 27B, scored higher than Flint.
The company acknowledged that Flint would need more guidance than the big paid coding assistants, and suggested breaking large tasks into smaller steps. Still, early reviews were positive. Wired’s Will Knight used Flint on a Mac with 48GB of memory to build several small programs, including a to-do list app and a tool that scours the web for research. He found that smaller coding models often ran into errors or were slow compared to Claude or Codex, but Flint nailed his coding requests every time.
The Eureka Machine comes up with ideas, runs experiments and uses the results to decide what to try next. According to the company’s launch video, it contributed to nearly every part of building Flint, from pre-training to post-training and inference.
Recursive said that Eureka’s contributions include a sparser model shape, low-bit training that shrank Flint by 71% with almost no loss in quality and custom kernels, which are specialized programs that speed up the underlying computations.
Recursive didn’t say how much time the Eureka Machine saved its researchers, but it’s not alone in leaning on AI to do research. OpenAI said last month that by mid-August, its AI agents were logging 3.1 workdays for every one worked by a human researcher.
If Recursive’s bet pays off, each new model should be able to take on longer stretches of work without human help. The company previously told TechCrunch that its $410 million compute deal with Amazon Web Services in June was “less about headcount and more about agent count.”
The longer-term goal, Socher told Wired, is for the Eureka Machine to achieve full recursive self-improvement, with humans overseeing the process and able to stop it if something goes wrong. Recursive says each new model should make the Eureka Machine a better researcher, helping it build the next one faster.

deep-tech-bd47999705.headline: Washington’s DeepSeek ban may deter US firms from adopting Chinese AI models: experts
deep-tech-bd47999705.fulltext:

The US government’s latest ban on Chinese artificial intelligence start-up DeepSeek could have a chilling effect on the wider American business community and deter companies from adopting low-cost Chinese AI models, industry experts say.
The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) ordered federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek products and third-party services built on the Chinese AI model from their IT systems, according to a directive signed in July and published on Monday.
The department also barred agencies from procuring such products, citing national security concerns.
China on Tuesday criticised the ban, accusing Washington of politicising trade and technology under the guise of national security.
Foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said Beijing opposed the overextension of national security concepts, while the commerce ministry called the ban a discriminatory measure that undermined fair competition, urging Washington to revoke it and warning that China would take necessary steps to protect its interests.
DeepSeek did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday.
While the DHS order explicitly targeted federal civilian agencies, its impact could extend to private companies that served both government and commercial clients, according to industry watchers.
Industry veteran Xiang Ligang, founder of Chinese telecommunications industry portal c114.com, acknowledged the need for government agencies to address security concerns, but warned against expanding the restrictions to the broader US market.
“DeepSeek is highly cost-efficient and the US should not shut it out, as doing so would be detrimental to the US economy and AI development,” Xiang said.
Making the DHS order public sent a clearer signal to companies beyond the federal procurement system, prompting software developers, cloud providers and systems integrators to assess whether their use of DeepSeek could jeopardise government business, according to an independent Chinese geopolitical and tech policy analyst who declined to be named.
The disclosure risked turning an internal government procurement restriction into a broader market signal, influencing how American companies designed their products and chose AI models, he said.
“This could change the cost calculations for American businesses when choosing AI models,” he added.
The move comes as US lawmakers seek to extend restrictions on Chinese AI models to private-sector suppliers serving government customers.
The growing regulatory burden is forcing American software developers to weigh the benefits of low-cost Chinese models against the risk of losing access to federal contracts.
The implications could extend beyond DeepSeek, according to the geopolitical and tech policy analyst, as the national security concerns cited by the DHS could in theory also be applied to other Chinese AI systems.
Washington was pursuing a multipronged strategy to counter the rising popularity of Chinese open-weight AI models, using procurement bans, defence supply chain rules and congressional scrutiny to raise compliance costs and political risks for American adopters, he said.
Those measures threaten to undercut the appeal of Chinese models, which have gained traction among US developers and businesses due to their competitive performance, low operating costs and flexibility for deployment on private infrastructure.
American firms have increasingly turned to Chinese-developed AI models to curb the soaring costs of deploying generative AI.
Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky has said the company uses Alibaba Group Holding’s Qwen models, citing their speed and affordability. Alibaba is the owner of the South China Morning Post.
Other prominent US tech players – including AI coding start-up Cursor, which was recently acquired by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, legal tech firm Harvey, and conversational engine Perplexity AI – have integrated models from DeepSeek or Moonshot AI.
For smaller developers, the savings can be particularly significant. A US-based developer told online tech publication Rest of World earlier this year that a coding task costing around US$10 using Anthropic’s Claude could be completed for less than 50 US cents using DeepSeek.
Beijing is also moving to tighten oversight of its own AI technologies flowing overseas.
China last week proposed new export controls covering advanced AI technologies and models amid rising security concerns, with some domestic industry figures calling for tighter restrictions.
Wang Yuquan, founding partner of venture capital firm Haiyin Capital, urged Chinese AI developers to shift towards closed-source models, arguing that open-weight releases exposed developers to foreign regulatory risks while allowing overseas platforms to profit from their technology.
Transitioning to proprietary models would help domestic developers retain control over deployment, reduce exposure to foreign bans, and build sustainable revenue streams, Wang was cited as saying in an interview with local media outlet Huxiu earlier this month.
Ben is a Beijing-based technology reporter for the Post focusing on emerging start-ups. He has previously covered Chinese tech for publications including KrAsia and TechNode.

deep-tech-7df6dc67b7.headline: India’s OSAT Buildout Puts Semiconductor Testing in Focus
deep-tech-7df6dc67b7.fulltext:
NI said Kaynes Semicon has selected its semiconductor test systems, while other Indian OSATs continue to evaluate equipment as manufacturers prepare for production.
With five semiconductor plants in India now in commercial production, the harder question is no longer if the country can package chips, but whether it can test them fast enough, across enough device types, to hit production targets.
The testing challenge arrives as global semiconductor test equipment sales are forecasted to grow 31% to $15.3 billion in 2026, following 55.3% growth in 2025, according to SEMI’s July 2026 forecast. The industry body expects sales to reach $20.8 billion by 2028, driven partly by increasing device complexity and more demanding performance and reliability requirements.
Against that backdrop, Indian outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) companies must accommodate different device types, meet production targets, and maintain test coverage as they scale. Some must modernize legacy testing platforms, while others need to develop test architectures from scratch for new chips.
When an Indian chip facility announces it can produce 15 million chips a year, that number says little about how many testers it needs. A chip tested in under a minute and one that takes five to 10 minutes can demand very different amounts of equipment for the same output.
In September 2025, Emerson announced a partnership with Kaynes Semicon to deploy its NI Semiconductor Test System (STS) as the primary test platform across Kaynes’ OSAT facility in Sanand, Gujarat. EE Times spoke with Karthik Balasekar, chief business manager for semiconductor and electronics, and Ved Mahanta, principal account manager, both at NI India, part of Emerson.
“Customers typically conduct tester qualification before making a final purchasing decision,” Mahanta said. “The process generally takes six months to one year. In the case of Kaynes, we can publicly state that the company has decided to proceed with NI testers. We are in the process of delivering the testers in the coming months.”
Mahanta added that discussions with other OSAT facilities were ongoing, with many still qualifying test equipment. NI could not identify some of these companies because their engagements were not publicly disclosed.
Balasekar said the number of testers also depends on the time required to test each device and the production target. “Facilities handling millions of devices may need fewer testers if each test takes less than a minute,” he explained. “Testing complex chips that require five or 10 minutes per device could demand more equipment to meet the same production target.”
Mahanta said, “An OSAT might announce an annual capacity of 14 million or 15 million chips, for example. Such figures generally represent the combined output capacity of its production lines, whether the facility operates 10 lines, 50 lines, or another number.”
Mahanta said NI Emerson has not publicly announced a specific number of test systems for Kaynes. He compared OSAT capacity announcements with those of automotive plants, which state how many vehicles they can produce annually. “Actual production depends on customer demand,” he said.
For relatively simple chips, pin count and the types of tests required are key factors. A chip with fewer pins and simpler testing requirements takes less time to test, allowing the same number of testers to process more devices.
In production environments, the priority is to test as many chips as possible in the shortest time while ensuring that devices meet their required specifications.
Mahanta said TestStand, NI’s test automation platform, automates test sequences to speed up decisions on whether a batch of chips is suitable for delivery.
Balasekar indicated that Kaynes’s selection reflects the need for test platforms that can accommodate different semiconductor device types. “Our STS is a platform that supports both mixed-signal and RF applications,” he said. “For example, if Kaynes tests mixed-signal products today and moves to RF products later, it can reuse the same STS tester for different devices under test.”
Flexibility is only part of the picture. The test architecture that an OSAT needs also depends on whether it is handling an established chip or a new design. “Typically, customers want to test two types of devices: legacy devices and new products, commonly referred to as new product development,” Mahanta said.
For legacy products, manufacturers may rely on older test platforms that can no longer deliver the required throughput. “OSATs need to move these products to newer systems without compromising test coverage,” Mahanta said, adding that customers often do much of the preparatory work and specify what the OSAT needs to test.
New designs present a different challenge, particularly when the customer is a semiconductor startup. “Some Indian startups developing their own chips have never performed final testing and depend on the OSAT to guide them,” Mahanta said. “The OSAT must help determine how to test each device reliably and quickly enough to meet production and time-to-market requirements.”
Although new devices do not carry the technical debt associated with legacy test platforms, they may require the OSAT to develop a test architecture from scratch. “This includes determining the test requirements, selecting an appropriate system, and ensuring that it meets test coverage and throughput targets,” Mahanta said. “Such a system could come from NI Emerson or another test equipment supplier.”
Both challenges—migrating established products to newer test platforms and developing test architectures for new devices—become more difficult to address with increasing design complexity, Balasekar said.
As semiconductor devices gain functionality, OSATs will need test systems that can accommodate evolving requirements without compromising existing test coverage. Mahanta said modular PXI (PCI eXtensions for Instrumentation) systems can allow customers to add modules for new tests without changing existing test parameters. “Customers can expand their testing capabilities as their requirements evolve,” he said.
For new devices, NI applies AI to parts of test development, including the initial design of test architectures.
Mahanta said an engineer could upload a chip’s datasheet to NI’s Nigel AI test development tool, which examines selected parameters and suggest a potential test architecture. “The engineer could then use the suggested framework as a starting point rather than developing the entire architecture from scratch,” he explained.
“This approach targets part of the work involved in test development, rather than replacing the validation engineer,” Mahanta said. “AI could take on some repetitive tasks, leaving engineers to focus on more complex problem-solving.”
Under India Semiconductor Mission 2.0 (ISM 2.0), the government will focus on building an ecosystem across six areas, including advanced packaging and testing units and talent, Ashwini Vaishnaw, India’s minister for electronics and information technology, said at SEMICON India 2026. For OSATs, that makes test system flexibility, device qualification, and the ability to accommodate different device requirements relevant to the industry’s next phase of growth.
Mahanta said NI has invested in local engineering capabilities so its engineers can support OSAT customers on site, reducing the need to bring specialists from Taiwan and Singapore. He also cited Tessolve, an NI partner serving customers globally, as an example of an Indian company participating in the testing ecosystem.
“There are integrated device manufacturers that base 40% to 50% of their product lines in India,” he said. “Building engineering expertise will be essential for Indian companies seeking to serve global semiconductor manufacturers.”
Balasekar said growth in OSATs and electronics manufacturing could outpace the availability of skilled workers. India’s exports of electronic devices and its expanding mobile phone manufacturing base add to the demand for talent. He pointed to the workforce development component of ISM 2.0 as one way to address the gap. “I think that will help India grow faster and keep pace with the market’s expansion,” he said.

climate-energy-9aa8fea839.fulltext:
China proposes ban on exports of perovskite, tandem solar manufacturing technology
China’s Ministry of Commerce (Mofcom) and Ministry of Science and Technology have proposed prohibiting exports of selected high-efficiency perovskite and tandem solar manufacturing technologies, alongside new restrictions on advanced polysilicon, wafer and crystalline-silicon cell production know-how.
The proposals, published on Oct. 16 under Joint Announcement No. 48 of 2026, would add 12 photovoltaic technologies to China’s Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export. They are part of a broader consultation covering 40 technologies across sectors including solar energy, artificial intelligence and biomedicine. The public consultation runs until Nov. 15.
The proposed export bans cover production processes and related equipment manufacturing technologies for perovskite-silicon tandem solar cells based on wafers measuring at least 182 mm and achieving conversion efficiencies of 30% or higher. They also include slot-die coating processes for perovskites with coating widths of at least 1.1 meters.
Additional thresholds apply to large-area modules, including single-junction perovskite modules measuring at least 1 square meter with conversion efficiencies of 18% or higher, and perovskite tandem modules of the same minimum area with efficiencies of at least 28%. The proposed controls target manufacturing technologies meeting these specifications rather than exports of finished modules.
Other technologies proposed for prohibition include cold-hydrogenation fluidized-bed processes for trichlorosilane production with annual single-line capacities of at least 250,000 metric tons, and silane-based fluidized-bed processes with annual capacities of at least 20,000 metric tons. The draft also covers processes for manufacturing silicon wafers no thicker than 70 micrometers and certain edge-passivation technologies for thin crystalline-silicon cells, along with related equipment manufacturing know-how.
The proposed restricted-export category includes polysilicon plant engineering technologies for production lines with annual capacities of at least 30,000 metric tons, as well as advanced crystal-pulling and wafer-cutting processes.
It also covers specified high-performance manufacturing processes for tunnel oxide passivated contact (TOPCon), back-contact (BC) and heterojunction (HJT) solar cells, including deposition, passivation, diffusion and metallization technologies. The HJT provisions include certain p-type technologies evaluated under air mass zero (AM0) illumination conditions relevant to space applications.
Under China’s technology import and export regulations, prohibited technologies cannot be exported, while restricted technologies can be transferred overseas only with government approval and the necessary licenses.
The proposed export bans and licensing requirements have not yet taken effect. However, a separate interim registration requirement took effect on Oct. 16, when the announcement was issued.
Companies must register planned exports of the listed technologies, including qualifying key equipment, through the Mofcom’s online system before transfer. The requirement covers intellectual property transfers, overseas technology licensing, changes in ownership or control involving foreign entities, and transactions that are underway but have not yet been completed.
The Mofcom said the proposals address national security concerns as photovoltaic technologies increasingly find applications in aerospace, defense and other sensitive sectors. The ministry said technologies that fall below the specified thresholds, as well as finished products manufactured using controlled technologies, are outside the proposed scope. It added that the measures do not target any particular country, region or company.
If adopted, the controls could reinforce China’s position in advanced PV manufacturing by limiting overseas access to some of its most sophisticated production technologies.
Although exports of finished solar cells and modules would not be directly affected, transfers of controlled manufacturing know-how through technology licensing, overseas production-line installation and commissioning, equipment exports and on-site technical support could be prohibited or subject to government approval.
In the near term, the measures could delay overseas PV manufacturing projects, increase compliance costs and limit the deployment of advanced Chinese production technologies abroad. Over the longer term, the restrictions could strengthen China’s influence over the international diffusion of next-generation PV manufacturing technologies, potentially slowing efforts by overseas manufacturers to close the technological gap.
However, tighter controls could also complicate Chinese manufacturers’ international expansion plans and heighten trade tensions or prompt retaliatory measures.

Unfazed by top conglomerates piling into data centres and buoyed by a successful public listing, Nashik-headquartered ESDS Software Solution Ltd is betting on renting out high-performance chips—critical to running artificial intelligence (AI)—to reach $5 billion in annual revenue within the next five fiscal years.
In an interview with Mint, Piyush Somani, chairman and managing director of ESDS, said even if the company “captures just 1% of the market over the next five years, our revenue would have crossed $5 billion”.
“Our aspiration is not to capture 50% of the market. That is how big the market is,” Somani added.
On 4 September, ESDS Software Solution went public with one of the steepest share price premiums in recent history driven by strong investor interest in AI and data centres. The company runs data centres, cloud platforms and rents out graphic processing units (GPUs)—expensive, high-power processing chips that run modern-day AI—to businesses and the Indian government.
ESDS listed at ₹908.40 per share, more than double its initial public offering (IPO) price of ₹429 per share. ESDS shares are currently trading at ₹1,434, up 3.4x over their IPO price and more than 60% since listing. The company’s current market cap is ₹16,800 crore.
ESDS ended FY26 with ₹472.21 crore in revenue, up 31%. To reach its targeted scale, the company needs to increase its revenue by 2.5x every year for the next five years. Such rapid growth is rare—barring the US tech giants and foundational AI firms such as Anthropic, which have grown even faster in the past three years.
To achieve such growth, Somani is eyeing deals such as its $1.25-billion, five-year GPU rental deal with Australian firm Sharon AI, signed in March. While the agreement could generate around $250 million annually for ESDS, it leaves the company exposed to the risk of upfront GPU investments if the client cancels.
When asked about that risk, Somani said the GPU capacity is currently fully contracted to clients, with more deals in the pipeline. If a client backs out, he believes ESDS can re-lease the unused capacity to new customers at higher rates, taking advantage of rising GPU prices to earn even better margins. Somani said the company receives substantial advance payments from customers, which it uses as its own equity contribution to fund projects, with only a small portion coming from debt and additional investor equity.
Betting big on AI infrastructure
Optimism around infrastructure providers like ESDS is being driven by rapid AI adoption, corporate cloud migration, and the rollout of 5G networks, all of which are sparking high demand for computing power in India. Running advanced AI models requires high-performance server capacity, while digital transformation demands reliable storage and processing.
ESDS is betting heavily on this demand. Despite rising GPU costs and global supply constraints, Somani expects ‘GPU-as-a-service’—where clients rent high-performance computing power—to generate nearly 75% of the company’s revenue in the near term, with data centres and other IT services contributing the remaining quarter.
Renting processors, which ESDS reports as infrastructure-as-a-service (IaaS), generated 44% of its FY26 revenue. This included cloud compute (33%) and data centres (11%). Managed cloud services generated 41%, and the remaining 15% came from selling software. The company operates five data centres across India, but did not disclose its operational capacity.
Somani, however, conceded that amid the euphoria around AI, adequate power supply is a key constraint. “Nowhere in the world are our customers getting enough power, and it has become the biggest limiting factor. We are focusing heavily on securing power allocations, and bringing more land with power access and powered buildings under our control.”
On 3 August, Mint reported about India’s power infrastructure shortage in the face of rising data centre expansion.
Competition in India's GPU-as-a-service market is growing, with domestic players such as Yotta, E2E Networks and Neysa expanding their businesses. They also face competition from global tech firms Amazon, Microsoft and Google, which offer computing services backed by much larger financial resources.
Somani said ESDS is not looking to compete for every customer. Instead, it wants to focus on areas where it believes it has an edge. “So our aspiration is to make sure that we are there in the competition for specific opportunities, select opportunities where the customer only believes that ESDS is the right player for me and ESDS can take care of my business,” he said.
Executive turnover & risk factors
Amid its ambitious growth plans, ESDS has already seen senior-level exits, with three C-suite executives departing over the past 18 months. Chief operating officer Jitendra Pathak resigned on 15 July, following the departure of chief technology officer Rushikesh Jadhav on 2 January. Rajeev Barnwal, chief autonomous cloud officer, stepped down on 16 June 2025, less than eight months into his tenure.
Downplaying the impact, management said the company maintains a strong internal leadership pipeline and that its core business model doesn’t rely on external CXO hires.
“We try to bring CXOs from the market, from other companies, from other cultures, assuming they will be able to manage our existing people. But then, you may not be 100% right while doing lateral hiring,” said Somani.
At least one brokerage said it sees growth potential for ESDS, but struck a note of caution. “We remain constructive on the long-term opportunity from sovereign cloud, AI infrastructure and rising GPU demand, supported by ₹3,000 crore order book,” analysts Kunal Bajaj and Rushil Katiyar of brokerage firm Choice Institutional Equities wrote in a 25 September note.
“That said, conversion of the pipeline, deployment timelines and utilization remain key variables, while the sharp scale-up in GPU capacity could also raise execution and funding requirements,” they added.

world-9f64e67e90.fulltext:
This is a “deepfake” of Brazil’s former right-wing leader endorsing his son’s presidential campaign, even though he is barred from posting online for trying to stage a coup.
Here is Uncle Sam, in a top hat and lugging a bag of cash, on a Brazilian beach while fighter jets swoop overhead and blast a nearby neighborhood.
And here are the two political rivals locked in a bitter battle for Brazil’s presidency, dancing side by side to a viral TikTok song.
Videos made with artificial intelligence, ranging from the amusing and absurd to the grim and deceitful, have flooded the Brazilian internet ahead of a high-stakes presidential election on Sunday.
This has turned Latin America’s largest democracy into a real-time laboratory for the electoral use of A.I., offering parallels to the United States, where critical midterm elections approach, and to other nations grappling with the effect of powerful new technologies on political life.
But in Brazil, a chronically online nation of 214 million where disinformation has defined elections for nearly a decade, the deluge of A.I. — made by candidates, strategists and ordinary citizens — has become a stark gauge of the nation’s capacity to police online content.
Online disinformation is already a hallmark of Brazil’s electoral season, but A.I.’s prevalence and advancing sophistication are posing a major new challenge for the Brazilian authorities working to protect the integrity of the country’s vote.
Brazil, which has some of the world’s strictest regulations against electoral falsehoods, has issued equally stringent rules on A.I. use during elections. But these guardrails have remained largely untested until now.
“We made the rules, now we’re watching to see what happens,” said Kássio Nunes Marques, chief justice of Brazil’s electoral court, which oversees the vote.

OpenAI has acquired Orchestra Bio, a platform that helps biopharmaceutical companies coordinate drug development programmes, as the company expands its AI tools for life sciences research. OpenAI has not disclosed the acquisition terms.
The acquisition will bring Orchestra Bio’s team and technology together with OpenAI’s Rosalind, a suite of AI models and tools for life sciences researchers. The companies plan to develop AI agents that connect scientific findings with the studies, decisions, and workflows required to advance drug candidates.
“Together, we aim to build agents that help teams connect scientific findings with the studies, decisions, and next steps needed to advance a potential medicine,” OpenAI said in a blog post announcing the acquisition.
Drug development takes an average of 10–15 years from target discovery to regulatory approval. The process involves multiple teams, external partners, and interconnected activities, often managed through separate systems.
Orchestra Bio’s platform allows scientists and programme leaders to delegate the monitoring and tracking of studies to AI agents, freeing them to focus on scientific decisions and resolving issues that could delay development.
Founded in 2022 by Ashoka Rajendra, Orchestra Bio helps biotechnology and pharmaceutical companies manage the operational complexity of drug development. The company developed AI agents to track studies, monitor drug development programmes, and identify issues that could delay clinical trials or other stages of development.
The startup had raised about $20 million by 2025 from investors including Andreessen Horowitz, Atria Ventures, and 8VC.
OpenAI said the acquisition would expand its efforts to apply AI across the drug development process. The startup said its GPT-Rosalind helps scientists investigate questions in biology and chemistry, while Rosalind Workbench connects AI capabilities with scientific tools and data to support research and experiment planning.
OpenAI is also working with pharmaceutical companies to apply AI to research and development. Its partnership with Novo Nordisk focuses on improving research and development and commercial execution, while its collaboration with Moderna involves using AI to translate insights from complex data into experimental workflows.

- Monsoon's gone, El Niño isn't: Why India's weather worries are far from over
Trending
El Niño is putting the world on alert, and India could be among the countries facing its next major weather test. After a monsoon marked by a 13 per cent rainfall deficit, attention is shifting to whether the climate phenomenon will bring a warmer winter, disrupt rainfall patterns and add to the pressure on agriculture.From Indonesia’s raging wildfires to an unusually active Pacific hurricane season, its effects are already emerging across the globe. Now, the question is what a strengthening El Niño could mean for India in the months ahead.According to the BBC, El Niño has been strengthening for several months and is already influencing weather patterns worldwide, with Indonesia experiencing its worst wildfire season since 2015, heightened hurricane activity in the eastern Pacific and reduced monsoon rainfall in India.The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) has warned that the phenomenon could intensify further towards the end of 2026 and persist into 2027, raising concerns over its potential impact on temperatures, rainfall and extreme weather events across different regions.For India, the immediate concern is whether the strengthening El Niño will compound the effects of the deficient monsoon and influence winter temperatures, rainfall and agricultural conditions in the coming months.
What is El Niño and how does it affect India's weather?El Niño is a climate phenomenon characterised by unusually warm sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean. It is the warm phase of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), a natural climate pattern that influences atmospheric circulation, wind systems and rainfall distribution across the world.For India, El Niño is closely watched because it is generally associated with a higher risk of below-normal southwest monsoon rainfall.The warming of Pacific waters alters atmospheric circulation and can weaken conditions that support the Indian monsoon, increasing the possibility of prolonged dry spells and rainfall shortages.While central India received near-normal rainfall, eastern and northeastern India recorded a 26 per cent deficit, classified as an exceptional drought, while southern states received 24 per cent less rainfall than average, according to the BBC.A strengthening El Niño could contribute to warmer-than-normal conditions in parts of India, potentially increasing pressure on water resources and agriculture.The World Meteorological Organization (WMO), citing the South Asian Climate Outlook Forum, projected normal to above-normal maximum and minimum temperatures across much of South Asia during October–December 2026.Higher temperatures later in the winter could also threaten wheat yields if heat coincides with the grain-filling stage, although the impact will depend on actual weather conditions.However, conditions in January and February will depend on evolving climate patterns, including western disturbances.
Global impact of El NiñoEl Niño is expected to push temperatures higher across much of the world while shifting rainfall patterns, increasing the risks of drought, wildfires and flooding in different regions.

Use four criteria, each scored from 0 to 5. Each criterion contains five checks. Each satisfied check earns one point. An unmet or unsupported check earns zero points. Do not use half-points for an individual judge’s checklist.
Judges are assigned to specific criteria. More than one judge may score the same criterion. Scores from those judges are averaged within that criterion before its weight is applied. Weights: Problem Value & Practicality 20%; AI Integration & Development 30%; Functionality & Reliability 30%; Design & Usability 20%. Let V, A, R, and D be the averaged scores, each between 0 and 5. Final score out of 100: 4V + 6A + 6R + 4D. A criterion’s weight does not increase because it has more judges.
V evaluates the proposed benefit and feasibility of adoption. A evaluates the use of AI in development and the implementation of AI within the project. R evaluates actual behavior and reproducibility. D evaluates how clearly a person can understand and operate the experience.

V2 — Supported need: A credible observation, firsthand example, user comment, or cited source supports the stated need or desired experience.

A3 — Input preparation: The implementation deliberately selects or prepares the inputs, context, retrieved information, or data supplied to the AI.
A4 — Task-specific configuration: The implementation includes prompts, instructions, model configuration, training, or other controls tailored to its intended AI task.
A5 — Output integration: The implementation contains a defined mechanism that passes AI results into a project feature, workflow, or action.
A1 can be earned through AI-assisted development. A2–A5 require AI integrated into the finished project. For A2–A5, assess the implementation and its purpose. Assess whether it produces correct, repeatable results under R. Using a particular provider, paying for a model, training a new model, or fine-tuning is not required.
Evaluate what the submitted project actually does. Score the value of its purpose under V, its AI implementation choices under A, and clarity of interaction under D.
R1 — Complete main workflow: The project can carry out its main task from start to finish and produce a usable result.
R2 — Result quality: Representative outputs meet the project’s stated requirements, supported by expected results, reference examples, or another suitable evaluation method.
R3 — Repeatability: The main workflow succeeds across repeated runs or representative cases. Where outputs vary, they still meet the required behavior.
R4 — Failure handling: At least one relevant invalid input, dependency failure, or foreseeable failure condition receives a controlled response rather than false success or an uncontrolled crash.
R5 — Reproducibility: The submitted code, dependency information, configuration guidance, and instructions allow another reviewer to reproduce the demonstrated behavior, with external service requirements identified.
Evaluate the submitted version. Clearly disclosed limitations should affect the relevant checks rather than automatically removing unrelated points.
Evaluate how clearly a person can understand and operate the project. Score whether the underlying functions execute successfully under R.
D1 — Clear entry point: The interface or immediate instructions make the project’s purpose and starting action understandable.
D2 — Clear task flow: The steps for the main task follow a clear sequence without unnecessary navigation or repeated input.
D3 — Useful feedback: The experience communicates relevant status, progress, and completion in understandable terms.
D4 — Readable presentation: Text, controls, and results are legible, distinguishable, and presented in a format appropriate to the project.
D5 — User control: Users can change inputs, restart, cancel, or repeat the main task through appropriate controls or instructions without developer intervention.
Apply these checks appropriately to websites, apps, command-line tools, games, and hardware experiences. Elaborate visual styling is not required. D5 evaluates whether an understandable control path exists. R evaluates whether the operation behind it works.

Government agencies and companies around the world shut down websites on Wednesday after two critical flaws came to light involving PHP, a programming language that is the basis for a large share of the internet.
PHP sits underneath popular web design platforms, so the weaknesses potentially affect a vast range of websites, from online stores and news outlets to government services.
Wiz, one of the security firms that found the issues, estimated that PHP runs about 70 per cent of the world’s websites and said the flaws rank “among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP and arguably in software history”.
The US National Security Agency told organisations to patch immediately or pull vulnerable systems offline. The flaws “often provide a direct path to the server’s file system or database”, the NSA said in a statement on social media.
Attackers could use them to take over web servers without needing a password.
Volker Dusch, a security engineer at the PHP Foundation, told The Wall Street Journal it was the most serious problem PHP had faced in more than a decade, comparing it to Heartbleed, a 2014 flaw that set off a worldwide rush to patch.
The discovery came amid a surge in software security disclosures driven by increasingly powerful AI models, with the number of vulnerabilities found in 2026 on track to roughly double last year’s record total.
“If you run PHP, it is imperative that you update now,” the PHP Foundation, which funds developers working on the language, said in a blog post.
Security firm Calif found the flaws in August using OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol model, as part of an OpenAI-funded audit of PHP’s code.
Google-owned Wiz said it found them independently weeks later with help from AI models including Google’s Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol.
OpenAI said on social media that it considered the bug “one of the most impactful vulnerabilities in recent memory”, adding that it “marks a new phase, where AI can find security bugs with internet-scale impact.”
Ethan Mollick, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School who studies AI, said that companies he talks to are struggling to keep up with the pace of patches needed to shield from AI-driven cyberattacks.
“Now consumers are going to have the same experience of getting everything updated often and fast,” he said on social media.
The flaws had been reported privately to PHP’s developers and kept confidential while a fix was prepared.
Details leaked online on Tuesday, a day before the planned release of the fix, prompting the rush to take sites offline.
In France, local government websites, including one for Paris police, have been inaccessible since Wednesday afternoon at the request of the French National Cybersecurity Agency, the interior ministry said.
In the Netherlands, the national digital identity service DigiD, the website of the House of Representatives and the site of the national cybersecurity centre went offline as a precaution, according to Dutch public broadcaster NOS.
Belgium’s foreign ministry temporarily took its websites offline as a precaution, it said on social media, although the Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium had recorded no attacks on Belgian sites.
In Australia, the Australian Signals Directorate said its own cyber.gov.au site was among government websites affected by the flaws, according to public broadcaster ABC.

Bobins Vayalil AbrahamPublished21 Oct 2026, 06:52 AM IST Two of the most valuable companies in the world are exploring a potential merger. Tesla CEO and founder of SpaceX, Elon Musk, on Tuesday said that they had formed special committees to discuss the merger between the two entities. While the size of the deal has not been officially announced, SpaceX is worth about $2 trillion, and Tesla is worth nearly $1.5 trillion, making the combined entity worth at least $3.5 trillion. SpaceX is currently the 7th most valuable company in the world, while Tesla sits in the 11th spot. "I think it would be a good idea, but it's really up to the special committees of both companies," Musk was quoted as saying by Reuters. Sharing further details about the potential merger, Musk said the special committees would discuss the matter while he sits out. "Because I'm a conflicted party, I can't actually be in the discussions of the special committees," which comprised independent directors, he told investors on a conference call, according to Reuters. “The companies had formed the special committees at the request of shareholders, who ultimately would need to approve a deal,” the world’s richest man added. As the CEO of both companies, Musk owns around a 20% stake in Tesla and 45% of SpaceX. Musk controls about 82% of SpaceX's voting power and would own about a third of the combined entity if the merger goes through. Tesla was founded in 2003 by Martin Eberhard and Marc Tarpenning and Musk joined the EV-maker as the lead investor in 2004. He was officially recognized as co-founder in 2009 as part of a legal settlement. Tesla’s vehicle portfolio included passenger electric cars, autonomous vehicles, semi-trucks and Robo-taxis. Tesla recently unveiled its latest offering, the Roadster, a high-performance sports car that can ‘fly’. SpaceX was founded in 2002 by Musk and currently operates under three segments: space missions, satellite internet services through Starlink, and AI under xAI. Musk pointed out the benefits of combining the two entities. "I do think there's a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there's a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software, chip design, the Terafab obviously, robotics, mass-to-orbit with the Starmind constellation, connectivity," he said. Terafab, the chip manufacturing joint venture between the two companies, should produce its first test chip around May or June of next year and aims to reach volume production by the third quarter of 2028, Musk said. He, however, made it clear that it would be premature to assume a SpaceX-Tesla merger would happen, noting that the special committees had not agreed on transaction terms and may never do so.
