Elon Musk said SpaceX and Tesla Inc have formed special committees to explore a potential merger, a preliminary step towards what would rank as the largest corporate tie-up of all time.
“I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies,” Musk, the chief executive officer of both companies, said on Tuesday on SpaceX’s earnings webcast.
“There’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software.”
Musk said he is not taking part in the committee discussions because he is a conflicted party, and that the committees have yet to agree on terms.
A blockbuster deal would unite Tesla’s electric vehicle, energy and robotics businesses with SpaceX’s rocket launch and satellite internet operations.
Underpinning it all are the companies’ shared ambitions in artificial intelligence – or what some in the industry are now calling superintelligence – fuelling investments in areas such as data centres and driverless cars.
Space computing: what is it, why move computing into orbit and where does China stand?
SpaceX shares rose 4.6 per cent in postmarket trading after reporting quarterly results, while Tesla climbed 1.2 per cent.
The scope of a potential merger is staggering, with both SpaceX and Tesla among the largest companies in the world and holding dominant positions in their respective industries.
SpaceX, formally known as Space Exploration Technologies Corp, has a market value of about US$2 trillion, while Tesla is worth nearly US$1.5 trillion.
SpaceX and Tesla already have numerous business ties, overlapping investor bases and even some shared personnel. The rocket maker has bought more than US$100 million worth of Tesla Cybertrucks, while xAI is a major customer of Tesla’s utility-scale batteries.
A combination has been widely expected since SpaceX rode a wave of investor enthusiasm to a record initial public offering this year, giving the company both currency and an implicit green light from shareholders to make a play for Tesla.
Bloomberg News reported in January that SpaceX had weighed a Tesla merger before ultimately deciding to acquire xAI, Musk’s artificial intelligence start-up.
Musk cautioned that a merger is not certain and would require shareholder support. He said Tesla would need approval from 50 per cent of all shareholders, rather than simply a majority of those voting.
“Some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty,” Musk said. “I think that would be overstating it.”

world-b17a25d8c4.headline: Elon Musk confirms he is considering merging Tesla and SpaceX
world-b17a25d8c4.fulltext:
Elon Musk confirms he is considering merging Tesla and SpaceX
- Published
Elon Musk has said he is actively considering merging Tesla and SpaceX, his two biggest companies.
"Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said during a call with financial analysts to discuss SpaceX's latest results on Tuesday.
While Musk noted it could not be assumed a merger will go ahead, and it would need shareholders' support, he said special committees within both companies had been formed to examine the move.
"The special committees have not reached agreement on terms of any transaction and there's no guarantee that they will," he said. "But I do think there is a lot of merit to merging and a lot to be gained."
With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5 trillion (£1.1 trillion) and SpaceX at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark one of the largest mergers in history.
SpaceX builds space rockets as well as Starlink internet satellites and provides a secured satellite network for governments, including the US, through its Starshield business.
That part of the business is currently facing scrutiny over claims Ukraine's access to the network has been limited, leaving it vulnerable to deadly strikes by Russia.
US President Donald Trump has denied either he or Musk ordered the slowdown. Musk himself suggested the US government might have been behind the restrictions.
Starlink's total revenue rose to $5.2bn in the three months to 30 September from $3bn in the same period last year. It is dwarfed by SpaceX's expansion into offering cloud compute capacity for other tech companies, such as Anthropic and Google.
The business generated revenues of $7.5bn over the three months, up from $813m last year.
- Why does Elon Musk want to merge Tesla and SpaceX? 
  - Published1 hour ago
'Tap dancing through a minefield'
Musk, who became the world's first paper trillionaire after the SpaceX stock market debut earlier this year, said he is not included in either of the special committees considering the mega-merger.
He described himself as a "conflicted party" as the chief executive of both Tesla and SpaceX.
Even commenting on the possibility of combining the two companies, Musk compared it to "tap dancing through a minefield".
A merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders, he added. At least 50% of Tesla's shareholders would need to approve a combination, which Musk described as "quite a high hurdle to achieve".
Shareholders have supported Musk's desires before. Last year, a majority of investors in Tesla approved a compensation package for Musk valued at around $1tn.
While Tesla is known as an electric car company, Musk has lately been shifting resources there to work around robotics.
SpaceX, with its growing focus on AI infrastructure, quickly outstripped Tesla on the stock market in terms of value when it made its market debut in June.
SpaceX, as a whole is not profitable, despite revenue jumping to $27bn from $13.7bn over the first nine months of the year.
Over that same period it lost $1.1bn although it did report a $4.4bn profit for the most recent three months.
Following Musk's comments, SpaceX's share price rose 8% in after-hours trading. Shares in Tesla, which reports its own quarterly results on Wednesday, rose by 2%
Over the last year, Musk has taken to bringing more of his companies under fewer banners. Before it went public earlier this year, SpaceX acquired xAI and X, the platform formerly known as Twitter, both of which Musk owned.
The recent launch of Terafab, a combined effort to manufacture computer chips between Tesla and SpaceX, was another signal that Musk sees his companies as potentially more effective when working together.
Musk said on Tuesday a full merger between the two companies would make sense for the work each is doing around chips, artificial intelligence and software.

Anthropic on Wednesday announced a preview of Claude Duet, an artificial intelligence agent that will likely challenge OpenAI's Dots and Meta's Muse offerings.
Claude Duet is designed for small businesses and professionals, Anthropic said. It can send users daily briefs, keep tabs on connected apps, and carry out a range of tasks like building dashboards, scheduling meetings and creating financial forecasts.
"It comes to you with what needs your attention, completes tasks you ask of it, keeps working even when you step away, and checks with you before it acts on your behalf," Anthropic said in a blog post.
The debut comes as competing products from Meta and OpenAI have started to show real traction with users. Meta's Muse, which the company touts as a "personal AI agent," launched last month and rocketed to the top of Apple's App Store. OpenAI introduced dots, its "always-on agents," during its annual developer conference weeks later.
Meta has primarily marketed its agent toward consumers, while OpenAI's product straddles both the enterprise and consumer markets. Anthropic said Wednesday that since Claude Duet is primarily designed for the workplace, personal errands, like booking tickets, are not "quite as strong."
Anthropic and OpenAI have long been fierce rivals, and they've spent much of the last year releasing competing models and jockeying for enterprise market share. Meta, meanwhile, has been revamping its AI strategy and pouring billions of dollars into new efforts to compete at the frontier. With the rise of personal agents, Meta is hoping to capitalize on the momentum.
Meta reported third-quarter earnings after the bell on Wednesday, and CEO Mark Zuckerberg told analysts that more 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada "have set up Muse personal agents" over the past month and a half. The initial success of the Muse helped Meta end September with its best month on Wall Street since 2022.
Anthropic said Wednesday that Claude Duet is still in an early phase, and that it "might misread a thread or miscalibrate what's urgent."
The company opened a waitlist for Claude Duet on Wednesday, and said eligible users will be able to access it through a standalone app or through the Claude website. Claude Duet is available to Pro and Max subscribers during the preview.

Canadian publisher drops writer Thelyson Orelien over AI use in novel
Publisher Boreal says investigations confirmed the Hatian-Canadian Thelyson Orelien used AI in his breakthrough novel.
The publisher of best-selling Haitian-Canadian writer Thelyson Orelien says it has severed its professional relationship with the author after confirming he used artificial intelligence to help write his novel, “It Was Either That or Die”.
Boreal said on Wednesday that it conducted a further investigation after allegations surfaced in September to determine whether AI was used to write the novel.
“New information, confirmed over the past few days, indicates that artificial intelligence was used in the writing process” of the novel, a Boreal statement said.
Orelien had previously denied allegations surrounding his breakthrough novel, and last week, the Canadian publisher said it was standing by the 38-year-old writer.
Boreal said it did not know the extent of AI’s use in the writing process “and we will likely never have a definitive answer”.
It said it gathered all the working versions of the novel and hired an outside party to analyse the various drafts.
“The results obtained this week revealed traces of AI tags in the metadata of certain documents,” Boreal said.
The publisher said it had tried to work with Orelien to gather the evidence necessary to prove his innocence.
That effort was inconclusive, and Orelien “subsequently announced that he would not provide any further information,” the publisher said.
‘Slander and heresy’
Orelien’s novel about migration, known by its original French title “C’etait ca ou mourir”, had been scheduled for translation in more than 20 countries.
France’s top book prize, the Goncourt, removed “C’etait ca ou mourir” from its shortlist after tests with the AI detector Pangram indicated a 100 percent probability that it contained computer-generated text.
But Orelien called the allegations “slander and heresy” in a statement sent to AFP earlier this month.
“Here and there I did use tools for research, particularly for foreign idioms,” he said.
“But not a single sentence in this book was created by a machine, nor the meaning or the structure of a story that comes from my gut,” Orelien said.
On Wednesday, he stood firm, telling the French newspaper Liberation that he had used AI “in the creative process” for “historical research”.
The author said he began writing the book in late 2017, before AI services such as ChatGPT were widely available.
When the allegations first surfaced in September, Orelien said he suspected racism was behind the attacks on him.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to resume US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine as soon as next month, the Kremlin said on Wednesday, after Putin met US envoy Steve Witkoff in Washington’s latest push to stop Europe’s bloodiest conflict since second world war.
The talks in a grand imperial palace in St Petersburg, the ninth time that Witkoff has met Putin in person, began with a goodwill gesture from Russia – the release of Stephen Hubbard, a retired US teacher held in Russia.
President Donald Trump confirmed the release in a social media post, saying the United States was not required to give anything in return.
Hubbard was first detained in April 2022 and was later sentenced to six years and 10 months on charges whose veracity his family and US-based lawyer question.
Wednesday’s encounter unfolded ‌amid concerns in Kyiv and among its allies that the US is backing away from Ukraine, at times holding back real-time intelligence on Russian attacks and hobbling Ukraine’s military communications.
The latest talks also came more than two years ‌after Trump promised in his successful election campaign to end the Ukraine war within 24 hours.
The Kremlin said the new three-way peace talks, which would be at a technical level, could take place in Abu Dhabi and would be focused on how to guarantee the security of Ukraine and Russia once the war ended.
They could begin sometime on or after November 10, it said. The last US-mediated peace talks took place in February before the US and Israel launched a war against Iran.
The Kremlin was less upbeat, however, about the outcome of talks Witkoff had held a day earlier in Oslo ⁠with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, the leaders of Finland and Norway and European and Nato representatives.
Witkoff told Putin the talks had been characterised by “some degree of momentum” and a US official said Ukraine had brought new ideas and proposals.
“These ‌nuances, so to speak, do not entirely satisfy us,” Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters after the St Petersburg meeting, which lasted nearly three hours.
Ukraine and Russia remain far apart when it comes to the terms of any possible peace deal, but Trump has recently intensified pressure on Ukraine to strike some kind of a deal. He said on Tuesday it was ‌time for Ukraine to end the war or face “a very bad thing”.
Putin also used Wednesday’s talks to offer to help Trump deal with Iran, saying Russia had a decades-long relationship with Tehran which it has repeatedly offered ‌to leverage to address US concerns about Iran’s nuclear programme.
Putin told Witkoff it was possible and necessary to get a deal with Tehran, the Kremlin said.
Russia could also supply large quantities of fertiliser to the US to help US farmers, the Russian president told Witkoff.
A potential meeting in China next month with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping was also discussed. The Kremlin said Beijing was already preparing what it said would be the first meeting of its kind in history.
Putin has shown few signs of compromising on his central ‌war aims, which ‌include full Russian control of the Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine, no Nato membership for Kyiv and an overall peace deal rather than a temporary ceasefire.
Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s special investment envoy, was also present at the meeting with Witkoff and the Kremlin said that major joint economic projects had been discussed, including some that were close to being realised.
Witkoff said he ‌had brought some documents with him containing various ideas for a potential peace deal for Putin to review, and that Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, also wanted to convey some ideas to Putin. Kushner later joined the meeting remotely by phone.
Zelensky said he hoped to discuss major issues about how ‌to end the war during a trilateral meeting with Putin ‌and Trump.
The Kremlin has repeatedly said that any Putin-Zelensky meeting would need to be painstakingly prepared in advance by aides to make it worthwhile.
US-Ukraine ties have deteriorated sharply since Trump announced a diesel export deal with Russia earlier this month to help lower prices in the US. High fuel costs since he launched strikes on Iran have hurt his Republicans ahead of November’s legislative election.
Since the diesel deal, Ukraine has complained of disruption to some intelligence-sharing and to its use of the Starshield military satellite system, though Zelensky ⁠said that Tuesday’s Oslo meeting had reached an agreement to resolve those issues.
Citing US officials and people familiar with the matter, The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that billionaire Elon Musk had last week ordered ‌the slowdown of a military-grade version of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite service that Ukraine relies on to track Russian ballistic missile strikes.
Musk has said any such decision is taken by the US military or the president. Trump has said he was not responsible and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio reiterated on Wednesday that Washington had not pulled back Kyiv’s ability to access Starlink.
